Ohm's law connects three things you can measure on a resistor: the voltage across it, the current through it, and its resistance.
It says voltage equals current times resistance, V equals IR . Know any two and you can find the third.
Engineers use it to predict how much current a given voltage will push through a part.
Think of water flowing through a pipe. Pressure is the voltage, the flow rate is the current, and a narrow section of pipe is the resistance. More pressure gives more flow.
A narrower pipe gives less flow for the same pressure.
The picture breaks down for some parts, such as diodes (one-way valves for current), where doubling the pressure does not simply double the flow.
Current flows out of the source's + terminal, through R, and back.
Measured with the passive sign convention (current entering R's + end), V R = +IR and the resistor absorbs P = VI = 25 milliwatts.
Voltage (V): the electrical "push" between two points, measured in volts.
Current (I): how much electric charge (the "stuff" of electricity, carried by tiny particles called electrons) flows past a point each second, measured in amps (A).
Resistance (R): how strongly a part resists current, measured in ohms (Ω). Resistor: a part made to have a known, steady resistance.
kΩ and mA: kilo-ohm is 1,000 ohms, and milliamp is one thousandth of an amp.
Put 5 volts across a 1 kilohms resistor. Current is voltage divided by resistance: I equals 5 over 1000 equals 0. 005 amps, which is 5 milliamps .
Double the voltage to 10 volts and the current doubles to 10 milliamps. Keep 10 volts but double the resistance to 2 kilohms and the current falls back to 5 milliamps.
That is the whole idea.
"Ohm's law is V equals IR : the voltage across a resistor is the current through it times its resistance, so I equals V over R and R equals V over I as well.
5 volts across 1 kilohms is 5 milliamps. It means current is proportional to voltage, a straight-line I–V curve.
The caveat is that it only applies to ohmic, linear elements at a steady temperature. Diodes and LEDs aren't ohmic, and a bulb's resistance changes as it heats."
